parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A sound wave is detected by a microphone that is connected to a cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO). The trace on the screen of the CRO is shown in Fig. 5.1.

{{figure:figure_5_1}}

Fig. 5.1

The time-base setting of the CRO is $2.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{s cm}^{-1}$.
parts.text: Determine the frequency of the sound wave.
hints: Hint 1: Look along the horizontal axis of Fig. 5.1 and count how many centimetres long one complete wave is, then think about what the time-base setting tells you about time per centimetre.
Hint 2: Convert that horizontal length into a time for one oscillation, then use the link between period and frequency to get $f$ in $\text{Hz}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the period from the screen**
You can read time across the screen because the time-base tells you how much time each centimetre represents. From Fig. 5.1 one full wavelength spans $6.0\text{ cm}$ horizontally. So the time for one oscillation is $$T = (\text{length of one wave}) \times (\text{time-base})$$ $$T = 6.0 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-5} = 1.2 \times 10^{-4}\text{ s}$$

Step 2: **Convert period to frequency**
Frequency is how many oscillations per second, which is the reciprocal of the period: $$f = \frac{1}{T}$$ $$f = \frac{1}{1.2 \times 10^{-4}} \approx 8.3 \times 10^{3}\text{ Hz}$$ That is about $8300\text{ Hz}$, well within the audible range.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text:
The intensity of the sound wave is now doubled. The frequency is unchanged. Assume that the amplitude of the trace is proportional to the amplitude of the sound wave.

On Fig. 5.1, sketch the new trace shown on the screen.

markscheme_points.text: new trace shows the same period
new trace shows amplitude of 10 small squares

hints: Hint 1: Think about what stays the same when only loudness changes - does the spacing of the peaks along the time axis change if frequency is unchanged?
Hint 2: Recall how wave intensity depends on amplitude, so doubling intensity does not double amplitude - what factor multiplies the vertical height?
parts.proper_answer: Same period (same horizontal spacing) with larger vertical amplitude increased by $\sqrt{2}$, to about 10 small squares peak to centre.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Keep the period the same**
Frequency is unchanged, so the time for one wave is unchanged. That means your sketch must have peaks and troughs at exactly the same horizontal positions as the original trace in Fig. 5.1.

Step 2: **Grow the amplitude by sqrt(2)**
For a wave, intensity $I$ is proportional to amplitude squared: $$I \propto A^2$$ Doubling $I$ means $$A_{new} = \sqrt{2} \times A_{old}$$ So the trace gets taller by a factor of about $1.41$. In small squares this takes the amplitude to about 10 small squares from the centre line. Draw the same sine shape, centred the same way, but taller.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text:
The time-base is now switched off.

Describe the trace seen on the screen.
hints: Hint 1: Picture what the time-base does - it sweeps the spot steadily left to right. If that sweep is turned off, in which direction can the spot still move as the sound signal varies?
parts.proper_answer: A vertical line (centred on the screen).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot with no horizontal sweep**
Normally the time-base pulls the electron beam horizontally at constant speed while the input voltage moves it up and down, painting a wave. With the time-base off there is no horizontal motion, only up and down motion from the microphone signal. The up-and-down movements overlap on the same spot, so you see a vertical line.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A beam of light of a single wavelength is incident normally on a diffraction grating, as illustrated in Fig. 5.2.

{{figure:figure_5_2}}

Fig. 5.2 (not to scale)

Fig. 5.2 does not show all of the emerging beams from the grating. The angle between the second-order emerging beam and the central zero-order beam is $16^{\circ}$. The grating has a line spacing of $3.4 \times 10^{-6} \text{m}$.
parts.text: Calculate the wavelength of the light.
hints: Hint 1: Focus on Fig. 5.2 - you are given the angle for the second order and the distance between adjacent slits. Think about the condition for constructive interference from many slits.
Hint 2: Rearrange that condition to make wavelength the subject, then substitute $n = 2$, $d = 3.4 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}$ and $\theta = 16^{\circ}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the grating law**
Light from neighbouring slits reinforces when the path difference equals a whole number of wavelengths. For normal incidence this gives: $$d \sin \theta = n \lambda$$ Here $n = 2$ for the second order, $\theta = 16^{\circ}$ and $d = 3.4 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}$.

Step 2: **Solve for wavelength**
Rearrange before putting numbers in: $$\lambda = \frac{d \sin \theta}{n}$$ $$\lambda = \frac{3.4 \times 10^{-6} \times \sin 16^{\circ}}{2}$$ $$\lambda \approx 4.7 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m}$$ This is blue-green visible light, a sensible size much smaller than the slit spacing.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Determine the highest order of emerging beam from the grating.
hints: Hint 1: Consider the largest angle at which a diffracted beam can still emerge - what is the maximum possible value of $\sin \theta$ for a beam just grazing along the grating?
Hint 2: Put that limiting value into the grating equation with your $d$ and $\lambda$ to find the theoretical maximum $n$, then decide how to round it to a real observable order.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Set the angle to its limit**
An order can only exist if $|\sin \theta| \le 1$. The highest possible order corresponds to $\sin \theta = 1$, i.e. $\theta = 90^{\circ}$: $$n_{max} = \frac{d}{\lambda}$$

Step 2: **Calculate and round down**
Using $d = 3.4 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}$ and $\lambda = 4.7 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m}$: $$n_{max} = \frac{3.4 \times 10^{-6}}{4.7 \times 10^{-7}} \approx 7.2$$ Orders must be whole numbers, and $n = 8$ would need $\sin \theta > 1$ which is impossible. So you round down to the next integer: $$n = 7$$
